issues.description: The problem statement (UML and text) requires the Animal class getter and setter for the name to have protected visibility, but the reference solution implements getName() and setName() as public. This mismatch can confuse students about the intended encapsulation level and whether they should declare these accessors as protected or public.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the visibility of the Animal class accessors consistent with the problem statement by changing getName() and setName() in Animal.java to protected. Update the solution (and any template examples) so the accessor methods are declared protected rather than public, ensuring subclasses in the same package can access them while external classes cannot.

issues.description: The UML in the problem statement indicates the Animal constructor should be protected (visibility '#'), but the reference solution declares the Animal(String) constructor as public. This contradicts the specified class design and may mislead students about intended constructor visibility and instantiation restrictions for abstract base classes.
issues.suggestedFix: Align the constructor visibility with the UML by changing the Animal(String) constructor to protected in Animal.java. Ensure subclasses (Seal, Pig, Goat) remain able to call super(name) — since they are in the same package this change is safe — and update template/solution code/comments to reflect the protected constructor.
